basis: Explanations are paraphrases of the game rules; tactical observations are commentary, not additional rules. Declared match interpretations are listed separately.

sections.title: 1.1 The normal victory condition
sections.text:
You win as soon as all of the opponent's holdings are destroyed. Do not finish the rest of a turn, offer a response window, or give the opponent a compensating attack after that condition has occurred. This is why a lethal Duelist / Wild Bill Hickok shot wins before retaliation and a lethal Rockslide Ridge strike wins before Rockslide Ridge destroys itself. Those two examples are expressly addressed by the current FAQ.

Crew are not additional lives. An opponent with six crew and no surviving holdings has lost. Conversely, a player with no crew can still win through holding abilities, Trouble, and hock effects. Count surviving holdings and accessible hit, not simply the number of cards on the table.

The current Land Office adds a separate victory condition tied to drawing the last card of the deck. The original Land Office did something entirely different. Chapter 11 distinguishes them. Do not import the old “start with only two surviving holdings” advice into a game using the revised Land Office.

sections.title: 1.2 The shared deck and its consequences
sections.text:
Both players draw from one shuffled deck. You do not build a personal deck before play, and you cannot assume that the opponent's cards come from a separate supply. Most non-named crew appear twice; the six named crew appear once each. Each of the ten ordinary Trouble appears twice.

This produces three practical consequences. First, a card discarded or played visibly changes what might remain available. Second, recovering a drifter into your hand can reveal a valuable card that neither player previously knew was being used as a body. Third, cycling the deck affects both players. Drawing heavily improves your options but also changes the pace toward a reshuffle or a Land Office finish.

The shared deck does not make memory perfect or authorize searching through old discards. The current FAQ permits examining what the opponent discards during their turn but forbids rummaging through the accumulated discard pile to reconstruct previous turns. Remembering public information is different from physically auditing the past.

sections.title: 1.3 A vocabulary worth learning exactly
sections.text:
Crew member / crew includes faceup crew member cards and facedown drifters. Enemy means an opponent's crew member, not an opponent's holding. Card in a combat effect is constrained by the effect and the cards in the battlefield; it is not permission to destroy a hand card, a queued Trouble, or a Hip Flask. Any usually removes the cover restriction for the specified class of target. It does not erase ownership or turn “enemy” into “holding.”

Hit changes an undamaged crew member or holding to damaged, or destroys an already damaged one. Wound does the same thing only to crew. Destroy removes a crew member or burned-out holdings a holding without requiring that it first be damaged, but a bare destroy icon still respects cover. Patch up repairs hit; it does not normally revive a destroyed card.

Ready means eligible to use an ability. Undamaged is a physical condition. The words are not synonyms. Damaged holdings can usually act; damaged crew cannot. A newly patched up crew member is undamaged but normally not ready. Its undamaged trait nevertheless works immediately. This distinction explains a large fraction of the questions in the casebook.

sections.title: 2.1 Standard setup, in order
sections.text:
1. Separate holdings from the shared crew-and-Trouble deck. Keep the two Stampede and two Whiskey Silos out of that deck.
2. Give each player their special cards and whiskey supply. Shuffle the main deck and the holding pool separately.
3. Deal six holdings to each player. Each secretly chooses three and places them in a row, then both reveal. Put the unused holdings away.
4. Draw each opening hand according to the total starting-card numbers on that player's chosen holdings. These numbers are not whiskey costs.
5. Determine the starting player with the whiskey-disc flip described in the rules. Begin the normal turn sequence; the starting player still draws during Replenish but collects only one whiskey on that first turn.

There is no general mulligan rule, no standard hand of a fixed size regardless of holdings, and no ordinary rule allowing holding selection after seeing the opening hand. A mutually agreed teaching or draft variant can change those things, but call it a variant.

Starting player is determined after the setup sequence. An older online discussion reached the same reading, but the important evidence is the order of the published procedure. Do not decide a holding's opening value under an assumed first-player assignment that the standard procedure does not yet provide.

sections.title: 2.2 The current recommended first-game holdings
sections.text:
The current booklet recommends Livery Barn, Rodeo Grounds, and Toll Bridge for the experienced player, and Cattle Ranch, Gatling Emplacement, and General Store for the other player. Use the card versions supplied with that booklet. Older tutorials show different introductory combinations, including the old Army Fort/Powder Magazine arrangements. A recently uploaded tutorial is not proof that its holding recommendations use the newest cards.

For a teaching game, place the holdings so their ability text remains visible. Explain starting cards before dealing the hand. Make a point of showing both abilities on a holding that has two. Teach one activation per card, rather than one activation per printed ability box.

sections.title: 2.3 Columns cover; they do not restrict your range
sections.text:
Each player normally has three columns, with a holding at the back and room for two crew in front. A crew member can be played before or behind the crew member already in that column. Where necessary, slide the existing crew member to make the legal arrangement. An ordinary ability can affect a legal target in any opponent column, unless its own wording gives a narrower restriction.

For example, a ready Annie Oakley / Sharpshooter in your left column can target a covered holding in the opponent's right column because Annie Oakley / Sharpshooter specifies any enemy card. A ready Vigilante in your left column can wound an exposed crew member in the opponent's right column. Neither unit is locked into a same-column duel. The column containing the attacker does not determine range.

If a rear crew member leaves, close the gap toward the holding as instructed by the rules. Do not preserve a fictitious empty shield space. Empty spaces never cover anything.

sections.title: 2.4 A simple position example
sections.text:
Read each line from the enemy-facing front toward the owning player's holding row:

 Left: Drifter -> Bartender / Piano Player -> Cattle Ranch
 Middle: damaged Gatling Gunner / Coach Guard -> Gatling Emplacement
 Right: General Store

The drifter is exposed; Bartender / Piano Player and Cattle Ranch are covered. The damaged Gatling Gunner / Coach Guard is exposed and still covers Gatling Emplacement. General Store is exposed. An ordinary hit effect may hit the drifter, damaged Gatling Gunner / Coach Guard, or General Store. An wound effect may hit either exposed crew member but cannot hit General Store. A suitable “any holding” effect can hit Cattle Ranch or Gatling Emplacement despite their screens.

Destroying the damaged Gatling Gunner / Coach Guard exposes Gatling Emplacement for a later, separate effect. A single ordinary hit icon does not spill through the Gatling Gunner / Coach Guard and hit the holding too. Cover is checked against the effect being resolved, not against a fantasy of surplus attack points.

sections.title: 2.5 Burned-out holdings and occupied columns
sections.text:
Destroying a holding flips it to its burned-out side. Its crew stay in play. The column remains available for crew, still normally with a capacity of two. The burned-out holding has no active ability or trait, but its existence can matter to cards such as Widow with a Shotgun / Homestead Defender and Homestead Cabin.

Boarding House is a specific expansion exception: it can remove a burned-out holding, allowing a crew member in the former holding position. This changes the space available in that column. It is not a general rule that destruction itself creates a third crew member slot. Riverboat and Wagon Fort are different exceptions: they change the holding's position within the column.

sections.title: 2.6 Full board replacement
sections.text:
If there is no space in any of your columns, an effect that brings in a crew member may first destroy one of your existing crew to make room. The condition is that the whole available board is full, not merely the column you would prefer to use. With a normal board, this means all six crew member spaces are occupied. With Boarding House, examine the actual expanded capacity.

The replacement option applies to ordinary plays and to incoming crew from effects, traits, Trouble, and hock. It is not a free-standing action to kill an inconvenient crew member whenever you like. You cannot clear a crowded preferred lane while leaving an ordinary empty space elsewhere. The published rulings clarify the “any of your columns” wording when introducing the change.

Destroying a crew member this way has real consequences. A faceup crew member goes to discard. A drifter goes facedown onto the deck. A destruction condition such as Boot Hill's can be satisfied. The incoming crew member then follows its own entry rules; it does not inherit the discarded crew member's readiness or status.

sections.title: 2.7 Public and private information
sections.text:
Hands are private, although a player may choose to discuss or reveal their own information in casual play. Holdings, faceup crew, Trouble queues, and the current state of whiskey use are visible. Drifters are facedown and normally cannot be inspected by either player. Do not peek at a drifter you created from the deck, even though it is on your side.

Wanted Poster Board specifically changes your access to your own drifters. Returning a drifter to hand also changes its status: it becomes an ordinary faceup-to-you hand card. Neither exception grants permission to inspect the opponent's other drifters or reorder the deck.

sections.title: 3.1 Trouble happen before your new whiskey and card
sections.text:
At the beginning of your turn, resolve the Trouble that is already in slot 1, if there is one. Then advance the remaining Trouble in your queue one slot forward. Only after that do you replenish: draw a card, then collect your three whiskey, except for the starting player's one-whiskey first turn. Then take actions.

The difference between “already in slot 1” and “moved into slot 1” is crucial. A Trouble beginning in slot 2 moves into slot 1 this turn and normally waits until your next Trouble phase to resolve. There is no automatic cascade that resolves every Trouble that touches slot 1 during the phase.

You cannot spend the forthcoming three whiskey to repair a holding before your queued Cholera or an opponent-benefiting effect resolves. You also cannot draw your replenishment card early and then decide how a Trouble should resolve using that newly revealed information. Preserve the order even when a casual shortcut usually seems harmless.

sections.title: 3.2 The five ordinary action types
sections.text:
During Actions, you can play a crew member or Trouble from your hand, spend two whiskey to draw a card, hock a hand card for its hock symbol, spend one whiskey to take your Hip Flask into hand, or activate a ready holding or crew member. You may repeat action types as often as the relevant costs and restrictions allow. The action phase is not “choose three actions” and not “play one card, then attack.”

Actions can be interleaved. You can hock for whiskey, play a crew member, activate a different card, draw, and then use the drawn card. You can activate an engine before sacrificing it. You can remove a screen with an wound hock effect and then use a holding to strike the newly exposed target. Sequence is a resource.

The freedom to repeat action types does not mean a single ready card can activate endlessly. Ordinarily, one use makes that card not ready. A card with two ability boxes chooses one when activated; using one normally shuts off both for the rest of that turn. Explicit exceptions such as Charles Goodnight and Chuckwagon are handled separately.

sections.title: 3.3 Paying and marking
sections.text:
Pay a crew member's play cost onto that crew member. Pay an activation's cost onto the activated card. For zero-cost plays and abilities, use a not-ready marker where appropriate. Put whiskey spent for actions without a continuing card in the whiskey discard area. This prevents spent whiskey from drifting back into the usable supply.

A marker is a bookkeeping aid, not the complete rules definition of readiness. A newly patched up crew member is not ready even if an old marker has disappeared. Conversely, an explicit effect may make a card ready while its earlier payment must remain accounted for as spent. Chuckwagon removes markers to show readiness; it does not refund their whiskey.

At the end of Actions, return the turn's whiskey and extra-whiskey discs to their supplies. Unspent whiskey is lost. Cards do not automatically heal during cleanup. Trouble stay in the queue. Hands have no size limit. A Hip Flask held in hand stays there.

sections.title: 3.4 Card traits and activated abilities
sections.text:
An ability is the text associated with an activation cost in a black ability box. A trait is an ongoing or triggered feature printed in the trait style. A faceup holding's trait continues while the holding is damaged, unless its own text says otherwise. A crew member's trait normally operates only while that crew member is undamaged.

Playing Argo, Vera, Zeto, or Quanah can therefore matter immediately even when ordinary newly played crew cannot activate. Restoring one of those crew patches up its trait immediately. That does not, by itself, grant an ordinary activation to the patched up crew member.

The cost is not the definition of an ability. A zero-whiskey ability is still an ability, still uses the card, and still matters to restrictions such as revised Church Bell Tower's “only ability” condition. A free hock effect, by contrast, is an action using a hand card's hock symbol; it is not an activation of that card's battlefield ability.

sections.title: 3.5 Do opponents get to interrupt?
sections.text:
There is no general reaction stack and no universal opportunity for the opponent to play from hand during your turn. The opponent makes choices or resolves effects when a card specifically instructs them to do so. Duelist / Wild Bill Hickok's retaliation and Gallows's unusual post-destruction ability use are examples. Do not import counterspell timing from another card game.

This makes threats on the board especially important. A ready lethal sequence is often final once Actions begins. The defense usually needed to happen on the preceding turn: hit the attacker, alter the queue, remove a trait, or change cover.

sections.title: 4.1 The target-selection procedure
sections.text:
Read the entire effect before picking a target. Identify the owning player, the type of object, any condition such as damaged, and whether cover is overridden. Then choose among the legal targets. Do not start with the most attractive victim and use the word “any” to justify it afterward.

For an ordinary hit icon, choose an exposed opponent crew member or holding. For wound, choose an exposed opponent crew member. For a bare destroy effect, follow its specified target type and normal cover. If the text specifies any, all, or one of a defined group, use that scope as directed. “All enemies in a column” means the opponent's crew in that column; it does not include the holding.

No friendly fire is the default. You cannot shoot your own crew member to create a convenient Boot Hill trigger or hock an wound card to hit your own Doc Holliday / Laudanum Doctor. A card must expressly authorize a negative effect on your own cards. You likewise cannot ordinarily patch up an opponent's card to create a more advantageous hit target.

sections.title: 4.2 Cover does not depend on health or readiness
sections.text:
A damaged crew member covers the cards behind it. A crew member played this turn covers immediately. A drifter covers despite lacking a printed ability. An exhausted crew member covers. A card need not be useful as an attacker to be useful as a screen. The rules diagram illustrates this directly: a sideways Claim Jumper / Jesse James is in front of Hellfire Preacher / Revival Sister, and only the Claim Jumper / Jesse James is marked exposed.

Nor is cover restricted to crew. Riverboat and Wagon Fort demonstrate that one of your holdings can cover a crew member behind it. The general definition asks whether one of your cards is in front of the target. It does not ask whether that front card is a crew member with a usable ability.

sections.title: 4.3 Hit is discrete, not a numerical health pool
sections.text:
A normal faceup crew member or holding has two relevant states before destruction: undamaged and damaged. One hit turns it sideways. A further hit destroys it. A direct destroy effect skips the intermediate state. Drifters are the exception: the first hit or injury destroys them.

Do not carry “excess hit” into the next card. Two separate hit effects can remove a front crew member and then strike the revealed card if each effect has a legal target when resolved. A single area effect, however, follows its own scope; it is not automatically a chain of freely retargeted shots. When multiple cards are named by the effect, apply the effect to those specified cards.

sections.title: 4.4 Patch up is not resurrection, and readiness is not restoration
sections.text:
Patch up rotates a damaged card upright. It does not return a destroyed crew member from discard, reveal a burned-out holding, or heal an unseen hand card. Original Roundup Corral was a specific exception involving burned-out holdings; the revised card has a different movement ability. Ordinary Patch up cannot imitate the old Roundup Corral.

A patched up holding may activate if it has not already used an ability that turn. Restoring a used holding does not reset its activation. A patched up crew member is normally not ready for the rest of the turn. Hot Springs and Chuckwagon create specific exceptions; apply the wording of the exception, not a general belief that all healing readies.

From v1.2 onward, a card cannot patch up itself. The prohibition includes indirect restoration generated by that card's ability. Apothecary and Smuggler's Landing cannot use a resulting patch up hock effect on themselves. The published rulings also address attempts to route self-restoration through activation helpers. An external card can still patch up the first card; the rule is not “a card that has been used cannot be patched up.”

sections.title: 4.5 What it means to leave and return
sections.text:
Returning a crew member to hand removes the battlefield object. Playing that card again creates a fresh entry with its normal cost, placement options, trait triggers, and readiness rules. It does not remember being damaged or used earlier in the turn. This is expressly stated for Sarah Winnemucca / Getaway Rider and Curfew.

That reset is powerful, but it is not free haste. Replay a normal crew member and it is normally not ready. Replay Sarah Winnemucca / Getaway Rider and its own entry exception applies again. Replay Blacksmith / Carpenter and its entry patch up happens again, even though it cannot ordinarily activate. Replaying Civil War Veteran / Buffalo Soldier Veteran repeats its entry draw and self-hit.

Moving a crew member within the battlefield does not normally mean playing it again. Jailhouse changes control without a new entry; the current FAQ explicitly says it does not trigger Civil War Veteran / Buffalo Soldier Veteran or count for Bordello. Roundup Corral changes position without an ordinary new play. Wanted Poster Board's flip, by contrast, expressly counts as entry. Preserve these distinctions whenever a holding asks what entered this turn.

sections.title: 4.6 Effects that cannot do everything
sections.text:
Do not invent a universal rule that every phrase must succeed before a card can be played. Pinkerton Agent / Lozen may enter even if no enemy Trouble can move backward. Patch up says you may patch up. Gain Drifter is optional. But named sacrifice and discard requirements can be prerequisites: Silver Mine, Undertaker, Dynamite Shack, and Railroad Work Camp require a crew member, and Pawn Shop requires two eligible hand cards.

For an unfamiliar compound effect, separate an explicit cost or condition from a following consequence. Then consult the card-specific ruling. “Destroy all your crew in this column” may act on an empty set in a way that “destroy one of your crew” cannot. Do not generalize from those superficially similar phrases without checking the relevant entry in the casebook.

When an effect contains several instructions, preserve their order and check for immediate victory at the point it occurs. You do not continue with an already-ended game merely because more text is printed after “then.”

sections.title: 5.1 Queue placement
sections.text:
A Trouble's printed timer is its initial queue position, not a cost and not an immediate number of turns to skip. If the printed position is occupied, place it in the first open position farther back, up to slot 3. You may not use an empty position in front of its printed position as a shortcut. If no legal position exists, you cannot play that Trouble.

Example: slot 1 is empty, slot 2 contains Stampede, and slot 3 is empty. A delay-2 Gold Rush goes into slot 3. If slot 3 is also full, you cannot put Gold Rush into empty slot 1. A delay-1 Run Out of Town could use slot 1 normally. Queue space is directional.

Delay-0 Trouble resolve immediately and are discarded; they never need an empty queue position. A full queue does not prevent playing Poker Night, Ambush, or Curfew. A trait that makes a Trouble delay 0 likewise changes how it is played; check whether that trait applies to the Trouble in question.

sections.title: 5.2 A complete countdown example
sections.text:
You play Cannonade at delay 3 during your Actions. On your next turn, it moves from 3 to 2. On the following turn, it moves from 2 to 1. On the turn after that, it begins in 1 and resolves before Replenish. It does not resolve on the turn it first moves into 1.

If an effect advances it from 1 during Actions, that can resolve it earlier, according to the effect. If a Trouble occupies the position directly ahead, an advance cannot jump over that Trouble. If Pinkerton Agent / Lozen pushes a Trouble backward, the impending resolution may be delayed; a Trouble that cannot move backward stays where it is.

sections.title: 5.3 Stampede are a reusable special Trouble
sections.text:
A spook the herd symbol either launches your Stampede or advances them. If they are outside the queue, a normal spook the herd effect places them at delay 2, using the normal placement rule if that slot is occupied. If Stampede are already queued, a spook the herd advances them one position provided the next position is open. If they are in slot 1, the spook the herd resolves them.

When Stampede resolve, the opponent chooses one of their holdings to take hit, even if covered. Your Stampede return to their special area, ready to be launched by a later spook the herd effect. They are not shuffled into the draw deck and do not remain permanently spent.

There is no once-per-turn cap on resolving spook the herd icons. Multiple separate spook the herd effects can launch, advance, resolve, and relaunch Stampede in one turn if the queue permits. The card producing an activated spook the herd ability may still have a once-per-ready-use restriction. Repeating the icon and repeating the same holding's activation are different questions.

sections.title: 5.4 Counting the work remaining
sections.text:
With an empty queue, Stampede outside the queue require three ordinary spook the herd icons to resolve entirely during one Actions phase: launch at 2, advance to 1, then resolve. Stampede already at 2 require two; Stampede at 1 require one. Natural Trouble-phase movement can reduce the number of paid or hocked spook the herd effects you need.

Coal Yard modifies the launch it produces to slot 3. Zeto may make the first Trouble played that turn immediate, including a newly launched Stampede Trouble. Cattlemen's Club discounts Trouble cards' whiskey play costs; it does not reduce the activation cost printed on Cattle Ranch or another spook the herd-producing ability. These are three different mechanisms, despite all involving Stampede.

Do not count three spook the herd icons as three holding hit. Under ordinary conditions those three icons generate one Stampede resolution. Conversely, do not count a Stampede card already in slot 1 as “still two turns away” because its usual launch position is 2.

sections.title: 5.5 Choosing which holding takes a spook the herd
sections.text:
The defending player chooses. A player often spreads hit to keep all holdings alive, but that is not mandatory or always best. Letting a weakened, low-value holding fall may preserve the health of a decisive engine. Keeping a nearly useless holding alive may provide another future choice for Stampede, yet also consume restoration resources that would better cover an attacker.

When every surviving holding is damaged, any Stampede resolution destroys one. Against a single surviving holding, the defender's choice disappears. This is why a spook the herd that seems modest early can become an unavoidable finishing threat late.

sections.title: 5.6 The Hip Flask is stored access to one extra whiskey
sections.text:
Spend one whiskey to take your Hip Flask into hand. Later, hock it for one extra whiskey and return it to its special area. You may hold it across turns. This converts an otherwise unused whiskey on one turn into access to a fourth whiskey on a later turn. It does not accumulate multiple stored waters inside a single Flask.

Buying and junking it in the same turn is normally resource-neutral. Repeating that loop creates no profit: you pay one and receive one. It can matter to bookkeeping or a specifically worded effect, but it is not an infinite-whiskey engine.

When an ability requires discarding non-Whiskey-Flask cards, your Flask cannot be used as a renewable discard payment. The distinction between junking a card and discarding a card matters here. Pawn Shop and revised Salvage Yard do not allow you to feed them a reusable Flask unless their wording actually permits it; their current wording excludes it.

sections.title: 5.7 Extra whiskey during Trouble or the opponent's turn
sections.text:
Ordinary cleanup returns whiskey at the end of your Actions, not at an invented universal beginning-of-turn wipe. Robbers Roost can produce whiskey when Stampede resolve. Gallows's Bartender / Piano Player example expressly lets the opponent retain the generated whiskey for use on their turn. Follow these specific timings even though the normal Replenish explanation says a turn begins with three whiskey. That statement describes ordinary supply, not a cancellation of an explicit effect.

This distinction is most relevant with the expansion. Keep newly generated extra whiskey physically separate from spent whiskey, and explain where it came from. A clear table state prevents arguments about whether a fourth whiskey was saved illegally or granted by a legitimate card effect.

cards.explanation:
Named crew member. Play 3; use 1; hock: drifter. Argo supplies a standard hit ability to your crew while his trait is active, and creates a drifter on entry. This can turn a board of screens and utility crew into several possible attackers. The attacks are still normal hit: cover applies, and each acting crew member needs readiness and whiskey.

Argo's immediate value includes the extra body and the abilities granted to crew who were already ready. The new drifter normally cannot attack that turn. A damaged Argo shuts off the granted ability; restoring him brings the trait back immediately without readying Argo himself. Argo retains the attack printed on his own card while damaged, so Saloon can use it. Hit switches off his granting trait and normal readiness; it does not erase his printed ability.

Use well: play him when existing ready crew can spend the whiskey you retain or generate. A three-whiskey play with no additional whiskey may threaten next turn but accomplish little now. Counterplay: hit Argo rather than clearing every new attacker individually. If the enemy's board already has good native attacks, prioritize the actual lethal line rather than assuming Argo must always die first.

Play 1; use 2; hock: spook the herd. Bounty Hunter / Tom Horn removes an exposed crew member outright. It is useful against a healthy, valuable exposed crew member because it avoids needing two hit effects. It cannot remove a holding, and it cannot reach a covered engine simply because its icon is Destroy.

Its activation consumes two thirds of normal whiskey. Compare that with cheaper injury that disables the same engine for the coming turn. The destruction is worth more when the enemy can patch up cheaply, when the body blocks a holding you can then finish, or when permanent removal prevents a recurring trait.

Use well: arrange a cheap screen removal first, then assassinate the valuable crew member behind it. Counterplay: put disposable bodies in front or make the Bounty Hunter / Tom Horn damaged before it gets a turn. In hand, its spook the herd hock may be the faster route to a holding win than developing a two-whiskey removal engine.

Play 1; use 0; hock: draw. Sacrifice one of your crew, then deal normal hit. The Leader may sacrifice itself. That makes it a whiskey-efficient conversion engine, but the sacrificed card or drifter is a real expense and may have been covering something important.

The best food is often a body that has already generated its entry value, a used utility crew member, or a drifter whose cover you no longer need. Use an eligible crew member's ability before sacrificing it when the sequence permits. Do not sacrifice a healthy ready attacker merely because the Leader's button says zero.

Counterplay: wound the Leader to switch off the conversion, or force its owner to keep every screen. Against Gallows, remember that the destroyed Leader is no longer available to sacrifice itself; the special post-destruction use requires another crew member.

Play 1; use 1; hock: draw. On entry it may push the opponent's Trouble one position backward where legal. Its attack is available when the opponent has a Trouble in play. The entry disruption can be valuable even if Pinkerton Agent / Lozen never activates, and it may be played when no Trouble can move.

The queue controls its value. A Trouble in slot 3 cannot be pushed farther; a backed-up queue can limit movement. Returning and replaying Pinkerton Agent / Lozen can buy additional time, but each replay costs whiskey and does not provide ordinary immediate readiness.

Use well: identify exactly which Trouble's resolution you must postpone. A delay that saves a decisive holding is worth more than a random annoyance. Counterplay: distinguish the disruption from the conditional attack. Sometimes resolving or removing your own queued Trouble switches off Pinkerton Agent / Lozen's attack condition; sometimes keeping the Trouble is still much more valuable.

Play 1; use 1; hock: draw. It destroys all damaged enemies, including covered damaged crew. It does not destroy damaged enemy holdings. This creates a strong second step after widespread injury, especially Cholera, but requires Regulator / Billy the Kid itself to be ready and undamaged when it acts.

A Regulator / Billy the Kid that is already on your board will itself be wounded by your Cholera. The attractive combination therefore needs a readiness/repair plan or a different timing arrangement. Merely placing the two cards next to one another does not prove the combo works this turn.

Use well: punish the opponent for leaving several disabled crew as screens, or pair with Gatling Gunner / Coach Guard/Ambush to create multiple damaged victims without injuring your own Regulator / Billy the Kid. Counterplay: patch up the important damaged crew member, remove Regulator / Billy the Kid, or recover crew into hand before the execution turn. Its draw hock is useful when there are no worthwhile damaged targets.

Play 1; use 2; hock: patch up. Gatling Gunner / Coach Guard wounds all exposed enemies. With the usual three columns, it can affect the front crew member in several lanes. It never wounds holdings. Box Canyon can make the opponent's rear crew exposed too, converting the attack into a much wider sweep.

Think of the first volley as a denial of future activations, not automatically as a board wipe. Healthy crew become damaged and still cover. A follow-up Regulator / Billy the Kid can remove them; another appropriately broad injury can also finish them.

Counterplay: heal the most important crew member, change which crew are exposed, or disable Gatling Gunner / Coach Guard before another volley. Drifters are especially vulnerable because the first injury destroys them. Do not spend two whiskey to wound several irrelevant bodies while an enemy holding engine is about to win unopposed.

Play 2 normally, or 0 in a column with your destroyed holding; use 1; hock: spook the herd. Widow with a Shotgun / Homestead Defender turns a lost holding into a discounted development location. The free play still follows normal entry readiness. It does not allow an immediate attack without another effect.

The discount is location-specific. A burned-out left holding does not make Widow with a Shotgun / Homestead Defender free in a healthy right column. If Boarding House removes the relevant burned out, do not casually retain the original discount; see open case C and the Boarding House entry.

Use well: develop Widow with a Shotgun / Homestead Defender in a burned-out lane as a cheap attacker and use the saved whiskey elsewhere. That lane can shelter the attacker behind another crew member even though there is no live holding to defend. Counterplay: exploit the time before Widow with a Shotgun / Homestead Defender is ready or accept its presence if a direct holding route ends the game sooner.

Named crew member. Play 3; use 1; hock: drifter. Her trait makes your crew enter ready, including Quanah. She turns extra whiskey and cheap crew into immediate action sequences. Without spare whiskey after paying three to play her, the readiness may be a threat rather than a current attack.

Quanah being patched up reactivates the trait but does not ready Quanah. New crew played afterward can still enter ready. This difference is explicit in the FAQ.

Use well: arrange Flask, Bartender / Piano Player, a whiskey hock, Trading Post, or another resource source before committing to a large entry chain. Account for the play cost and activation cost of every new crew member. Counterplay: hit Quanah as soon as possible; her trait can be more dangerous than her own hit ability. A covered Quanah plus retained cards threatens plays that are not yet visible on the board.

Play 1; use 2; hock: whiskey. It deals normal hit and draws a card if that hit hits a holding. Claim Jumper / Jesse James rewards access to holdings and can turn pressure into continuing options. Hitting a holding does not need to destroy it to qualify for the draw.

Its two-whiskey attack competes with an ordinary draw action, but can provide both hit and a card when the lane is open. Against a wall of crew, the economic bonus may be unavailable. This makes a cover-removal effect or a cheap opening strike particularly valuable.

Counterplay: screen the vulnerable holding or disable Claim Jumper / Jesse James. Do not automatically spend more cards covering a low-value holding than the Claim Jumper / Jesse James trigger would have earned. In hand, its whiskey hock is a common way to reach a four-whiskey turn or fund a final activation immediately.

Named crew member. Play 3; use 2; hock: drifter. Magnus hits all cards in one opponent column. This reaches the holding and crew in that column, so piling precious assets behind the same screen can expose them to a concentrated blow.

The attack costs two whiskey after the three-whiskey investment to play him. Without Quanah, Railroad Depot, Chuckwagon, or another valid timing route, he normally gives the opponent a turn to respond. He is formidable when covered and already ready, but an expensive crew member left exposed can be shut down by a cheap injury.

Use well: select the column whose combined losses matter most, not necessarily the one with the most bodies. A healthy holding becoming damaged may create a future Stampede finish. Counterplay: hit Magnus, move critical crew if you can, or avoid concentrating every useful trait in one lane.

Play 1; use the copied ability's cost; hock: wound. Con Man / Bass Reeves copies one ready friendly crew member's ability or an undamaged enemy crew member's ability. It does not copy a holding or an entire trait. Self-reference points at Con Man / Bass Reeves, and the original source is not used up by the copying.

This is an ordering card. Copy your ready Rustler / Drover before Rustler / Drover spooks the herd. Copy a ready Molgur before Molgur destroys a holding. Copy Sarah Winnemucca / Getaway Rider to return a different crew member before the actual Team acts. If you activate the friendly source first, it may no longer be legal to copy.

Counterplay: remove the best source, wound Con Man / Bass Reeves, or keep your own powerful crew member damaged when that is less costly than offering its ability. The published rulings confirm that copying another Con Man / Bass Reeves does not unlock an unready friendly source; case A explains the ruling and its history.

Named crew member. Play 4; use 1; hock: drifter. Molgur destroys any enemy holding, covered or not. A surviving ready Molgur threatens a complete holding every turn at very low activation cost. The expensive play and normal readiness delay are the opportunity to stop him.

A Flask or whiskey hock can pay the fourth whiskey for deployment, but that does not automatically leave whiskey for an immediate activation or supply readiness. Calculate the entire route. Copying a ready Molgur with Con Man / Bass Reeves, or readying Molgur with Chuckwagon after a use, can produce multiple holding destructions if the whiskey and timing work.

Counterplay: wound or remove him before his next action phase, interrupt the haste enabler, or win first. Ordinary screens in front of your holdings do not solve his targeting. Because he costs four, delaying his deployment by attacking resources and tempo can be as useful as saving a direct answer.

Play 1; use 0; hock: wound. Bartender / Piano Player generates extra whiskey. A covered Bartender / Piano Player can expand later turns' budgets, but normally does not refund its own play cost immediately because it enters not ready.

The value depends on how many useful activations it survives to make. If the opponent spends a cheap injury to disable it at once, your development may have gained little. If it supplies the extra whiskey for a decisive named crew member or a second removal effect, it can be central to the game.

Use well: cover it when the additional whiskey changes what you can do; activate before sacrificing or returning it. Vera can extend its production under her normal trait rules. Con Man / Bass Reeves can copy its zero-cost ability. Counterplay: hit it when that actually prevents a meaningful four-whiskey sequence, not merely because generating resources looks threatening.

Play 1; use 0; hock: wound. Its ability can hit, patch up, or do both, then hits Doc Holliday / Laudanum Doctor itself. The patch up cannot target Doc Holliday / Laudanum Doctor under current rules. An ordinary use from undamaged leaves it damaged; activating a damaged Doc Holliday / Laudanum Doctor through an authorized helper can destroy it with the self-hit.

Doc Holliday / Laudanum Doctor compresses several useful effects into a zero-whiskey activation, but readiness and self-hit are its real limits. Restoring it normally does not let it activate again that turn. Rescue/replay also needs an entry-ready effect to produce another immediate use.

Use well: choose both beneficial effects when legal, then recover or sacrifice the disabled body later. Counterplay: force its owner to invest whiskey in resetting it, or finish it if its body is opening a holding. Do not overpay to kill a Doc Holliday / Laudanum Doctor that has already done its work if another target controls the next turn.

Play 1; use 1; hock: wound. Barn Burner / Railroad Saboteur hits an exposed enemy holding. It is a cheap holding finisher with a narrow access requirement. A crew member in front of the holding prevents the ordinary attack even if that crew member is damaged or useless.

Use well: combine with screen removal, Box Canyon, or movement that opens a lane. Keep one whiskey for the Barn Burner / Railroad Saboteur shot after paying to clear the blocker. A plan that spends all three whiskey exposing a holding but cannot fire is incomplete.

Counterplay: place even a cheap drifter in the threatened lane, hit Barn Burner / Railroad Saboteur, or use the knowledge of the required lane opening to force an inefficient exchange. Against Box Canyon, screening alone is insufficient for that turn. Its wound hock can sometimes create the holding access needed by a different attacker.

Play 1; two one-whiskey options; hock: spook the herd. Choose between gaining a drifter and a normal hit attack available while you have a drifter. Without an exception, using the first box makes the card not ready, so you cannot then use its second box in the same turn.

The card supports its own condition over multiple turns and pairs naturally with other drifter generation. The threshold is at least one drifter, not one in Ringleader / Trail Organizer's own column. A copied attack checks the copying player's drifter condition.

Counterplay: destroy the last drifter to switch off the hit option when doing so is efficient. Be aware that another drifter can be generated from hand hock or a holding, so do not treat the absence of drifters at the start of Actions as permanent cover.

Play 1; use 2; hock: wound. It patches up on entry and has a later two-whiskey patch up ability. Its entry effect can repair a holding immediately while also adding a body, making it particularly useful when you cannot afford to wait for an ordinary new crew member's activation.

The bot's entry patch up does not normally ready the healed crew member. Its own activation cannot patch up itself under the current prohibition. Returning it to hand and replaying it generates another entry patch up, paying the play cost each time. Sarah Winnemucca / Getaway Rider and Con Man / Bass Reeves can make that sequence efficient when correctly ordered.

Counterplay: decide whether to stop the recovery engine or finish the covered target before another turn. Damaging the bot disables its activated ability but does not retroactively undo the patch up it already supplied on entry.

Play 1; use 0; hock: wound. It enters ready and returns one of your crew to hand, including itself or a drifter. Recovery removes hit and use history by creating a fresh hand card; replay still requires normal cost and entry rules.

This is a flexible engine for repeated entry effects, saving a valuable damaged crew member, uncovering a drifter's real card, and changing where a crew member is later replayed. Returning a front screen can expose your own holding, so complete the positional calculation before celebrating the recovered card.

Counterplay: wound the Team before the next turn, pressure its owner's whiskey, or threaten a holding that cannot tolerate the screen leaving. Gallows destroys the Team before its special activation and therefore prevents self-rescue in that specific case. Ordinary self-rescue remains legal.

Play 1; use 1; hock: spook the herd. Discard the top three deck cards and optionally use one of their hock effects. It offers selection among symbols without putting those cards in your hand. The unchosen symbols are not also gained.

Prospector / Assayer's value depends on what kinds of immediate effects would help. It is a flexible tool rather than a reliable promise of a particular hock symbol. If a drifter was just destroyed onto the top of the deck, part of the next reveal may be predictable, but do not peek at hidden faces to acquire that knowledge.

Use well: activate when several outcomes are useful, or when deck manipulation supplies a known good top card. Counterplay: do not assume its random activation will always produce the one answer you fear. Distinguish discarding deck cards from drawing them when current Land Office is in play.

Play 1; use 1; hock: whiskey. Rustler / Drover generates a spook the herd icon. It is a repeatable clock against holdings even when the opponent has excellent crew cover. Like any newly played normal crew member, it must survive to readiness before its ordinary activation.

The card is strongest when its spook the herd advances a meaningful threat: Stampede at 1, an active spook the herd engine, or a plan to repeatedly force hit onto the last holding. A Rustler / Drover activating into a blocked queue may accomplish nothing, so inspect the next slot first.

Counterplay: hit it if that prevents the critical Stampede resolution. Removing it after Stampede have already reached 1 may be too late if the opponent has a spook the herd hock available. In hand, the whiskey hock can be worth more than developing a repeatable spook the herd source when this turn's budget is the immediate bottleneck.

Play 1; use 2; hock: patch up. Annie Oakley / Sharpshooter hits any enemy crew member or holding, ignoring cover through its target wording. It is one of the most direct answers to a sheltered trait engine and can finish a damaged holding behind a full wall.

One hit disables a healthy crew member's trait and ability but does not remove the body. Decide whether that temporary shutdown solves the next turn. Against a holding, one hit may only create a restoration obligation; a second hit or another unavoidable hit source makes the threat much stronger.

Counterplay: hit Annie Oakley / Sharpshooter, patch up a key target, or force the two-whiskey activation to compete with defense. Stacking more crew in front of an Annie Oakley / Sharpshooter target does not stop it. A patch up hock held in hand can save a holding without requiring the Annie Oakley / Sharpshooter itself to survive deployment.

Play 1; use 1; hock: spook the herd. Duelist / Wild Bill Hickok creates a drifter on entry. Its attack deals normal hit, then lets the opponent deal normal hit back. The retaliation is immediate, follows targeting rules, and is not restricted to Duelist / Wild Bill Hickok. A lethal holding hit wins before retaliation.

The entry supplies two bodies for one play: Duelist / Wild Bill Hickok and the drifter, if accepted and legally placed. This is useful for covering multiple locations or satisfying entry/population conditions. The attack should be evaluated as an exchange, not a free one-whiskey shot.

Use well: attack when their returned hit is harmless, when your own hit is more valuable, or when it is lethal. Counterplay: preserve a threatening retaliation target on the enemy side, and remember that you choose a legal target rather than automatically damaging the unit that fired.

Named crew member. Play 3; use 1 for wound; hock: drifter. Her trait lets a card remain ready after its first ability use in the turn. The extra opportunity still requires legal readiness before that first activation and enough whiskey for another use. It can benefit Vera herself, other crew, and holdings.

Vera is especially dangerous with zero- and one-whiskey engines because the normal three-whiskey budget otherwise limits the value of extra activations. A twice-used two-whiskey attack needs a fourth whiskey. A newly patched up Vera supplies the trait immediately, but cannot resurrect earlier spent activations retroactively.

Counterplay: hit Vera before the opponent's engine turn. If you cannot reach her, pressure the limited whiskey or remove the best beneficiary. Do not assume her own wound ability can hit holdings; the trait is often the holding-killing component because it amplifies another card's attack.

Play 1; use 1; hock: spook the herd. Vigilante provides a simple cheap injury against an exposed enemy crew member. Its efficient activation can switch off a resource engine or trait while leaving whiskey for development or another attack. It cannot hit holdings.

Use well: disable the crew member whose next activation would matter most, or finish a damaged front crew member to expose a holding for another effect. The difference between those two tasks is strategic: one denies tempo, the other changes access.

Counterplay: use a disposable screen, patch up a critical trait, or accept the injury if the crew member was never central to your next turn. Against a player with no useful crew member targets, Vigilante's spook the herd hock can still contribute directly to the actual victory condition.

Play 1; use 1; hock: wound. On entry, draw a card and then hit the Soldier. It supplies an immediate replacement card and a damaged body that still covers. The entry trait is not an ordinary activated draw that you may repeat without replaying the crew member.

Its natural partners are sacrifice engines, recovery, and Saloon. The Lab can activate a damaged Soldier that entered this turn, paying the Soldier's ability cost, then destroy it. Ordinary restoration alone leaves it not ready.

Railroad Depot can also use its attack after the entry hit. Pay one to deploy it, draw, hit it, pay one for its attack, resolve that attack, then apply the Base's hit, which destroys it. The published rulings corrected an earlier ambiguous explanation of this sequence.

Use well: treat the body and the card as separate benefits. A wounded screen can be enough to preserve a holding, or it can become hit through a sacrifice engine. Counterplay: do not spend a premium removal effect on a body that has already replaced itself unless clearing that screen creates decisive access.

Named crew member. Play 3; use 1; hock: drifter. Its trait makes the first Trouble played each turn delay 0. Its ability draws three and then requires discarding three eligible hand cards, so it filters options rather than generating three permanent extra cards. The discard selection is broader than Poker Night's “of these cards” restriction.

Zeto's trait applies immediately while undamaged, including to a newly launched Stampede. It does not accelerate already queued Trouble. Sequence your first Trouble carefully: spending the benefit on a naturally immediate Trouble can waste the opportunity to resolve a major delayed Trouble now.

Counterplay: hit Zeto before the Trouble burst. If it arrives with only the three normal whiskey spent, consider what extra-whiskey sources remain. Its presence is dangerous, but not every hand can immediately pay for Cannonade after the three-whiskey deployment.

Play 1; delay 1; hock: spook the herd. Destroy any enemy crew member. Cover does not shelter the chosen crew member, but holdings are outside its target class. The delay gives the opponent time to use or recover the threatened asset, and the target is chosen when the Trouble resolves rather than permanently marked when the Trouble is played unless an effect expressly says otherwise.

Run Out of Town is attractive against a covered expensive engine that ordinary attacks cannot reach. It is less attractive if the opponent can make the board's only important crew member disappear or win before resolution. Zeto can remove the usual waiting period when Run Out of Town is the first Trouble played under the active trait. Compare the immediate spook the herd hock with the future removal before committing.

Play 4; delay 3; hock: patch up. Hit the opponent's holdings, then draw according to their destroyed holdings. Its reach bypasses crew screens. Its cost exceeds the normal three-whiskey supply, and its delay invites disruption. A four-whiskey play that does not affect the battlefield for several turns can lose a race before paying off.

Its best uses either compress the delay through Zeto or Telegraph Office, attack an opponent who cannot finish quickly, or establish an unavoidable future finish against damaged holdings. Earlier burned-out holdings still count for its ordinary draw condition. Boarding House's removal creates the separate inference discussed in open case C.

Counterplay includes Pinkerton Agent / Lozen, pressure that forces the Cannonade player to lose first, and restoration before the hit lands. When your own holding is about to die, the patch up hock can be more valuable than the Trouble's spectacular potential.

Play 1; delay 1; hock: wound. Each player, starting with the Trouble's controller, destroys all but one of their crew. The surviving crew member is chosen by its owner. Holdings remain. This punishes large populations while allowing a single valuable engine to remain.

Use it when you have fewer useful bodies to lose or can exploit the resulting open holdings. The order of choosing can reveal which enemy crew member remains before later actions occur, but do not turn the Trouble into targeted removal of the opponent's best crew member: they choose what to keep.

Counterplay includes sacrificing expendable bodies for value before the Trouble resolves, recovering crew into hand, and preserving the one crew member that matters to your next turn. Building a fresh crowded board immediately before your own Hard Winter is often wasteful.

Play 0; delay 1; hock: whiskey. Rearrange your crew, and make the opponent's cards exposed for that turn. The rearrangement may leave the formation unchanged. The exposure is the critical offensive effect; it converts ordinary targeting into access to previously sheltered crew and holdings.

Box Canyon does not itself deal hit. You need ready attackers, useful hock effects, and sufficient whiskey when it resolves. Preparing a Gatling Gunner / Coach Guard, Barn Burner / Railroad Saboteur, or cheap holding attack in advance matters more than simply playing the Trouble whenever it is drawn.

Counterplay targets the coming attack sources, changes the race, or delays the Trouble. Do not expect more screens to stop an effect that removes cover for the turn. The whiskey hock, however, may be the exact resource needed for a current lethal line rather than a delayed setup.

Play 1; delay 0; hock: whiskey. Look deeper into the deck by drawing four, then discard three of those four. You keep one of the newly drawn cards. You cannot keep all four and discard three older hand cards instead.

This is immediate selection, not raw hand growth. It can find a needed hock symbol, a finishing Trouble, or a crew member that suits your holdings. It also advances the shared deck substantially. Compare its cost with simply junking it for whiskey when you already have the right play in hand.

With Cattlemen's Club's discount it can become cheaper to use, but the first-Trouble interaction with Zeto still matters: a naturally immediate Poker Night can consume the trait's first-Trouble opportunity. Order your other Trouble first if that delay reduction is more valuable.

Play 2; delay 1; hock: patch up. Destroy the enemies in one column: the opponent's crew, including covered ones. The holding is not an enemy and survives the Trouble itself. Prairie Fire creates access for later holding hit rather than supplying that hit directly.

The threat discourages the opponent from stacking two valuable crew in one lane. They may recover or move crew before resolution, so count both the eventual destruction and the defensive actions you force.

When it resolves before Replenish, the newly opened holding is available for your following action phase if no intervening effect changes the position. Reserve a ready attacker and whiskey plan. A Prairie Fire that clears a lane but leaves you unable to exploit it may still be useful, but it is not automatically a holding kill.

Play 2; delay 1; hock: spook the herd. Wound all crew on both sides. Healthy faceup crew become damaged; already damaged crew and drifters are destroyed. Holdings are unaffected.

Cholera can disable a whole engine board, remove a drifter wall, or prepare a mass execution. It can also shut off your own Argo, Vera, Quanah, and Regulator / Billy the Kid. Plan the post-Trouble board explicitly. The classic Cholera/Regulator / Billy the Kid idea requires a way for Regulator / Billy the Kid to act after the injury or a deployment sequence that avoids the injury.

Counterplay is often to extract value before the Trouble lands, recover the most valuable crew member, or keep useful cards in hand for afterward. Restoration of a trait may be valuable even when the patched up crew member's own ability remains unavailable.

Play 2; delay 0; hock: draw. Immediately wound all exposed enemies. This resembles Gatling Gunner / Coach Guard's attack without requiring a ready crew member, but spends the Trouble card. It can disable several exposed crew and removes exposed drifters in one action.

Because it is immediate, it can be used after a different action changes cover. With Box Canyon active, the opponent's normally covered crew become eligible too. It still cannot wound holdings.

Counterplay occurs before the turn: cover key crew, disable the exposure setup, or avoid presenting several valuable exposed targets. During the action itself there is no general opportunity to play a response card. When only one minor crew member is exposed, the draw hock may produce a more useful option.

Play 2; delay 0; hock: wound. Return all crew to their owners' hands. Drifters become normal hand cards. Holdings stay in play, usually suddenly exposed. Replayed crew have fresh state and ordinary entry costs and readiness.

Curfew can erase the opponent's expensive board investment, rescue your damaged crew, turn drifters into real options, and expose a final holding. But it also gives the opponent their crew back and may reveal valuable cards from their drifters. It is a reset, not permanent destruction.

Use it before a holding-based finishing attack or with a cheap replay engine. Count the remaining whiskey: after paying two, one ordinary whiskey remains. A ready one-whiskey holding attack can capitalize immediately, while a two-whiskey attack needs an extra source.

Play 1; delay 2; hock: wound. Gain up to three drifters as the effect permits. These are crew and can cover holdings, satisfy population thresholds, feed sacrifices, or gain abilities from Argo or Gunsmith. The current full-board rule permits replacement to make room; older lists that simply forbid excess drifters are outdated.

It offers efficient bodies but delayed impact. The opponent can plan around the arrival, and broad injury can remove all three. Decide where each drifter produces the most cover or synergy rather than filling lanes mechanically.

Against Timber Ram or Bunkhouse, population can become offensive rather than merely defensive. Against Cholera, the same population can be fragile. The wound hock remains a useful immediate option when waiting two queue steps is too slow.

Starting cards 1; use 0, plus the crew member's ability cost. Activate one of your damaged crew, then destroy it. The FAQ permits a newly entered damaged crew member or one that has already acted. The Lab converts an otherwise disabled asset into one final activation; it does not waive the crew member's whiskey cost.

Civil War Veteran / Buffalo Soldier Veteran is a natural partner because it arrives damaged after replacing itself with a draw. A damaged high-impact crew member can also produce a last useful effect. The cost includes losing the body and its cover, so activate only after considering the lane it opens. The Lab's zero cost leaves whiskey for the chosen ability and a follow-up action.

Against it, injury alone may fail to deny the enemy's decisive effect. Permanent removal or pressure on the Lab itself can be necessary. Do not assume every damaged crew member is inert when this holding is active.

Starting cards 1; use 1. Hire a drifter while you have zero or one crew. Drifters count as crew for that threshold. With one crew member, one activation can reach two; after that the condition no longer holds. A second activation through Vera still checks the population again.

Livery Barn supports a lean board and recovery after losses. It works well with sacrifice holdings because consuming a body can reopen its condition. It is less useful while you maintain a large covered army. In selection, ask whether your plan regularly wants few crew or whether Livery Barn will sit idle behind five bodies.

The opponent can sometimes avoid killing an irrelevant second crew member so Livery Barn stays switched off. This is a useful example of why removing every possible enemy card is not automatically good play.

Starting cards 1; use 2. Patch up a damaged crew member and make that crew member ready. Unlike ordinary patch up, this explicitly recovers an activation opportunity. It repairs no holdings. The two-whiskey cost means a one-whiskey ability on the patched up crew member fits the ordinary three-whiskey turn; a two-whiskey ability needs extra whiskey.


This holding turns a damaged Molgur, Rustler / Drover, or other important one-whiskey attacker into a current threat. It can also reset a self-damaged Doc Holliday / Laudanum Doctor. Do not compare it with a one-whiskey Blacksmith / Carpenter play solely by the shared healing outcome: the readiness exception is the Garden's distinguishing value.

Counterplay may require destroying the crew member rather than injuring it, or damaging the Garden's holding again when it is already damaged. A single injury against the enemy's best attacker can be only a temporary tax while this holding survives.

Starting cards 1; use 0. Destroy one of your crew for extra whiskey. You need a crew member, and a drifter qualifies. It turns board material into a larger current action budget.

The best sacrifice has already produced its useful effect or would soon be destroyed anyway. A spent Bartender / Piano Player, damaged Soldier, or spare drifter can bridge a critical whiskey gap. The worst sacrifice may be the only screen keeping your last holding alive. Whiskey has no value if the extra action does not improve the position enough to justify the loss.

With Vera, additional conversion opportunities require additional crew. Zero activation cost does not mean zero material cost. Against the Bank, evaluate the opponent's board as potential whiskey as well as potential cover.

Starting cards 1; use 0. Hit Logging Camp, then patch up any number of eligible damaged cards. Logging Camp itself cannot be patched up at all under its printed restriction, including by another card. That is stricter than the general rule against self-restoration.

Logging Camp trades its finite health for a broad recovery. A large repair can save several holdings and reactivate several undamaged traits, though patched up crew normally remain not ready. Do not mistake mass healing for a free turn of mass attacks.

Its second self-hit can destroy it. If it is your last surviving holding, that destruction loses the game before a later benefit can save you. Use its remaining health as a planned consumable, and do not include it in an external-healing loop that its text forbids.

Current: starting cards 1; use 2. Produce a spook the herd and a drifter. The two effects provide holding pressure and a body in one activation. The spook the herd still obeys queue restrictions; the drifter still uses available capacity.

This is an efficient mixed-purpose action when you want both effects. It is less efficient than a one-whiskey spook the herd when the body is unnecessary, or than a cheaper drifter source when the queue is blocked. Bunkhouse, sacrifice engines, and population conditions improve the value of its drifter.

Current: starting cards 2; use 2. Starts damaged; can hit an enemy target only while Army Fort is undamaged. An external patch up unlocks its attack. Once healthy, shooting does not hit Army Fort.

Its extra starting card helps compensate for the initial repair requirement. Pair it with a reliable restoration route or be prepared to use its opening hand contribution while delaying the attack. It is a poor assumption that “damaged holdings can act” overrides this specific undamaged condition.

Starting cards 0; use 2. Hit any enemy card, then destroy one of your crew. Despite the sacrifice occurring later in the wording, the FAQ requires a crew member to use the ability. A drifter qualifies.

Dynamite Shack supplies valuable access to covered crew and holdings. The cost is two whiskey plus a body, so it excels when that hit is decisive or the sacrificed crew member is expendable. It can finish a covered damaged holding without first clearing two screens.

Counterplay includes removing available fodder, pressuring the Dynamite Shack's health, or making its owner choose between a necessary defensive body and the attack. Do not overbuild cover around a holding if the opponent already has the Dynamite Shack payment ready.

Current starting cards 1; legacy starting cards 2. Use 3 minus your number of drifters, minimum 0. The attack is normal hit. The revision changes the starting hand contribution, not the main discount mechanism.

Three drifters can make an activation cost no whiskey. Those drifters remain crew and can be vulnerable to broad injury. The discount is recalculated when you use the ability; a destroyed drifter can change the budget immediately. More than three drifters do not create negative costs or generate whiskey.

Use cheap drifter production to make holding pressure affordable alongside other actions. Against it, removing the third drifter may be more valuable than injuring a random attacker because it changes the entire enemy turn's whiskey arithmetic.

Current: starting cards 1; use 1 to move a crew member, or 2 to spook the herd. Movement may affect either player's crew member, even a covered one, but keeps it on the same side and requires a legal destination with room. Normal insertion may push an existing crew member.

Moving an enemy screen can open a holding or expose a valuable crew member. Moving your own crew member can improve cover or prepare a column condition. The spook the herd option ensures the holding still has a useful role when movement cannot help. Remember that the two abilities are alternatives under ordinary readiness.

Starting cards 0; use 1. A simple spook the herd source. Cattle Ranch asks little of your hand or population and works while damaged. Its zero starting-card contribution is a real setup cost, particularly when paired with other zero-card holdings.

Cattle Ranch is useful from the first turn, but a first-turn spook the herd into an otherwise empty queue is setup, not immediate holding hit. Combine it with future natural movement and hock spooks the herd. It can also exploit Zeto's first-Trouble trait when it launches Stampede under the ordinary rules.

Counterplay requires understanding the whole spook the herd clock. Destroying Cattle Ranch can remove repeatable pressure, but a Stampede already at 1 may still resolve from hand hock. Do not spend all resources on the holding while ignoring an immediate lethal finish.

Starting cards 0; use 1. Advance the holding through its column; on the third move it returns to its starting position and the opponent destroys one of their holdings. Crew can end up behind it, covered by the holding. The FAQ explains insertion around it and its return to the holding row when destroyed.

This is a visible countdown to defender-chosen holding destruction. The opponent can see how close the third activation is and must decide whether to destroy Riverboat, race, or accept a holding loss. Vera can compress the activation schedule if her trait is already active and conditions permit.

Its moving cover makes position unusually important. A valuable crew member behind Riverboat may be sheltered from ordinary hit while the holding itself is exposed. Any-target effects can still reach the crew member. Track moves physically rather than using a vague “nearly ready” memory.

Starting cards 1; use 0. Sacrifice one of your crew, then patch up another eligible damaged card. The FAQ requires a crew member to activate it. It cannot patch up itself.

Railroad Work Camp converts expendable population into survival or trait recovery without spending whiskey. It is useful when you have a damaged important holding and a body whose continued presence is less valuable. A recovered crew member's trait can matter immediately, but its ordinary ability remains not ready.

Against it, pressure the supply of fodder or threaten two damaged holdings so a single repair cannot solve everything. A player with Railroad Work Camp and a nearly empty board may be easier to overwhelm than its zero-cost healing first suggests.

Current: starting cards 0; use 2. Hit any enemy holding while you have at least four crew. Cover does not stop the shot. The population condition makes bodies part of your offensive infrastructure.

Drifters, Duelist / Wild Bill Hickok, Gold Rush, and cheap Holdouts can support the threshold. A fourth crew member placed this turn counts even when not ready. The ability does not require four ready or undamaged crew. Counterplay can remove the fourth body or hit the holding itself when close to destruction.

Starting cards 0; use 0. Destroy one of your crew to draw a card. A crew member is required, and drifters count.

Undertaker turns spent board material into hand options. It can be useful after an entry trigger, after an activation, or before an expected board wipe. Sacrificing a drifter places it on top of the deck, so the subsequent draw can retrieve that actual card. This is a consequence of the drifter destruction rule and the effect's sequence, not permission to inspect it earlier.

The zero starting-card contribution matters. Pairing Undertaker with no reliable body supply can produce a holding that has little to do. Against it, force the owner to keep screens in place or punish an exposed holding after a greedy conversion.

Starting cards 1; use 1. Deal normal hit after at least two crew entered your play this turn. Drifters count. Duelist / Wild Bill Hickok's crew member plus its created drifter can establish the condition, and replaying a crew member can contribute fresh entry Trouble. Jailhouse recruitment does not.

The holding rewards turns that already develop bodies. Its cheap attack can follow those entries if enough whiskey remains. A condition based on entries is different from a condition based on total current population: two older crew standing around do not qualify.

Counterplay is partly predictive. An opponent with a hand full of cheap crew or an imminent Gold Rush may have easy access to the shot. Do not assume the holding is inactive merely because no one has entered at the start of the action phase.

Starting cards 1; trait. Your crew cost one less to play into this column while it contains no crew. The discount is tied to the empty column, not to your entire board. Costs do not become negative.

Trading Post helps cheap entry-effect crew produce value with little or no whiskey. Sarah Winnemucca / Getaway Rider can repeatedly return itself, keeping the column empty between plays. Blacksmith / Carpenter can be replayed cheaply if a separate recovery route clears it. But a crew member left in the column switches off the next discount.

This is a strong example of space acting as an economic resource. Filling the Trading Post lane with a permanent defender can be correct for survival, yet it closes the discount engine. Against it, recognize that an apparently empty lane may be deliberately preserved for efficient development rather than forgotten cover.

Current: starting cards 1; trait. Win when the last card is drawn from the deck while the trait applies. It creates an alternate objective and forces the opponent to respect deck pace. Being damaged does not normally disable a holding trait, so one hit does not remove the threat.

The strategic plan is not simply “draw as fast as possible.” You must keep Land Office alive and avoid losing your other holdings before the trigger. Distinguish drawing from milling or creating drifters; see open case E.

Starting cards 1; use 1. Advance any Trouble one position when the space ahead is empty. A Trouble at 1 can resolve through the advance. The Trouble may belong to either player and remains owned by that player.

This holding turns whiskey into time. It can make a delayed attack arrive before the opponent can repair, or resolve a prepared Box Canyon during Actions. It can also advance an opponent's Trouble, sometimes beneficially and sometimes disastrously. Read whose crew or holdings the Trouble affects before touching the queue.

Counterplay includes blocking useful advancement with queue structure where relevant, disrupting the Trouble, or forcing the owner to spend whiskey elsewhere. The Clock does not make the original Trouble card free and cannot jump it over another queued Trouble.

Starting cards 1; use 2 to spook the herd or 2 to patch up. A flexible holding that can advance the holding-hit clock or repair another damaged card. The two abilities share ordinary readiness. It cannot patch up itself.

Stagecoach Station's value comes from having a relevant option in several game states. Its spook the herd is more expensive than Cattle Ranch's, but it contributes an opening card and a repair mode. Choosing holdings is not merely selecting the lowest number next to a familiar icon.

Use its repair when it prevents a holding loss or recovers a crucial trait; use its spook the herd when continued defense only delays an inevitable loss. Against it, apply enough pressure that one repair per turn cannot maintain all important assets, or exploit the two-whiskey cost by developing faster.

Starting cards 1; use 0 plus play and ability costs. Play a crew member and use its ability through the holding, then hit that crew member. The FAQ explicitly requires both whiskey payments.

The holding converts a hand card into an immediate activation, bypassing the normal wait for a newly played crew member. It is therefore a threat multiplier even when the battlefield contains few ready attackers. A one-whiskey crew member with a one-whiskey ability fits into two whiskey; Molgur's four-plus-one sequence requires substantially more.

The later hit leaves a disabled but protective body, or can destroy a crew member already damaged through its own entry effect. Evaluate the entire sequence before choosing the card. Against this holding, do not judge the opponent's available attacks solely by what was ready at the start of their turn.

Starting cards 1; use 3 minus your destroyed holdings. Deal normal hit. With one burned-out holding it costs two; with two it costs one. The discount creates a stronger late-game holding without making the loss of other holdings automatically desirable.

Homestead Cabin can anchor a comeback when the opponent has spent resources destroying lesser holdings but left this engine alive. It still needs legal exposed targets. A healthy opponent board covered by many crew may require hock or a Trouble to open access.

Boarding House's removal of burned-out holdings can change the discount under the component-based interpretation discussed earlier. Preserve a clear board state. Against Homestead Cabin, consider whether finishing it directly is better than destroying a different holding and making its surviving attack cheaper.

Starting cards 0; use 2. A straightforward normal hit attack with no special condition. It is easy to teach and provides a stable way to convert whiskey into pressure.

Its activation is not especially cheap, and its lack of opening cards can make a holding combination slow. Its advantage is reliability: no population threshold, no sacrifice, no incoming-crew member requirement, and no need for a Trouble to have resolved. Use the remaining one whiskey for a body, a spook the herd from another source, or Flask preparation when appropriate.

Against Gatling Emplacement, ordinary cover works. A damaged crew member can absorb the next shot, though the owner may have a hock effect to clear it first. Do not mistake the simple text for low strategic value when a guaranteed attack is precisely what the opponent needs.

Starting cards 1; use 2. Destroy Powder Magazine and all crew. This is a mutual crew wipe paid for with one of your holdings. It does not destroy the opponent's holdings.

Powder Magazine can punish an opponent who invested heavily in crew while you retained useful hand cards or holding attacks. Its activation should leave a plausible winning position afterward. Blowing up your last holding loses; clearing the board does not compensate for having no surviving holdings.

Counterplay can involve holding crew in hand, extracting value before the wipe, or forcing Powder Magazine to be used at an unfavorable time. A visible wipe also changes bluffing: the opponent may intentionally keep their board lean, which can give your normal attacks better holding access without firing Powder Magazine at all.

Current: starting cards 1; use 1. Normal hit, but it must be the only ability you use that turn. The restriction covers zero-cost abilities and abilities used before or after it. Non-ability actions remain available.

This supports turns built around playing cards, hock, and one efficient attack. It conflicts with an engine plan that relies on Bartender / Piano Player, multiple holding activations, and crew member attacks in the same turn. Its low cost should be evaluated together with the opportunity cost of shutting off those other abilities.

Current: starting cards 1; use 0. Discard one non-Flask card, then hire a drifter or an extra whiskey. The discarded card's own hock effect is not also gained. This holding converts any eligible hand card into one of two resources.

It smooths a hand with the wrong symbols and can supply the fourth whiskey for a critical turn. A card already offering the desired hock is usually better hocked directly unless a separate reason matters. With Vera, more conversion requires more cards; the holding does not create resources from nothing.

Starting cards 0; use 1. Hit an opponent card chosen by that opponent. The choice wording provides its own target procedure; it is not your targeted one-whiskey hit to any card you prefer.
