Its strength rises when every available choice is unpleasant. Against many healthy disposable crew, the opponent may absorb the hit cheaply. Against a sparse board of damaged holdings, the same activation can be decisive. Pressure-choice effects become more reliable as you reduce the opponent's harmless alternatives.

Counterplay includes preserving a low-value hit recipient and avoiding a position where every choice loses a critical card. Do not assume that a cheap activation necessarily gives its controller precise control over the hit distribution.

Starting cards 2; use 2. Draw two and discard one of those two. It gives a larger opening hand and a selective replacement for the ordinary two-whiskey draw action. You do not keep both new cards by discarding an unrelated old card.

General Store supports consistency and access to the right hock symbol. It can be valuable in a slow turn when no current attack is worthwhile, but repeatedly drawing without developing pressure can concede the game. Its two-whiskey activation competes directly with many attacks.

Counterplay is often tempo rather than targeting the Depot first. Force the owner to answer threats so they cannot comfortably spend two whiskey selecting cards every turn. A holding that improves future options is less useful when the next enemy turn is already lethal.

Starting cards 0; use 1. Destroy one of your crew; the opponent then destroys one of theirs. You choose your payment, and they choose their loss. It is not targeted assassination of their best crew member.

The exchange improves when your expendable drifter faces a single valuable opposing crew member. It worsens when the opponent has a spare drifter of their own. Against an empty enemy crew board, it offers no useful enemy sacrifice and does not hit holdings.

Use other removal to reduce their cheap alternatives before activating if the whiskey budget permits. Against it, keeping one low-value crew member can shelter an important engine from the choice effect even if ordinary positional cover would not matter.

Current: starting cards 2; use 2. Deal normal hit if this column contains two of your crew. Those crew need not be ready or undamaged. The condition rewards defending the holding with a full ordinary column.

The combination of two opening cards and an attack makes it a stable development holding, but losing one local crew member switches off the attack until replaced. Population elsewhere does not qualify. Moving a crew member away to improve another lane can therefore have an offensive cost.

Starting cards 2; use 1. Patch up after at least two crew entered your side this turn. Drifters count, while a Jailhouse recruit is not a new entry. It cannot patch up itself.

This holding combines a generous opening hand with conditional cheap healing. It fits turns that naturally play Duelist / Wild Bill Hickok, generate multiple drifters, or replay entry-effect crew. The restoration can save a holding or patch up an important trait; it does not normally ready a healed crew member.

Against it, recognize that population already on the table is not enough. If the opponent has an empty hand and no entry engine, the condition may be difficult to satisfy. Conversely, one Duelist / Wild Bill Hickok play can be enough to switch it on when its drifter is accepted.

Starting cards 1; use 2 to wound or 2 to spook the herd. The offensive crew-control icon is Wound, not Hit. It cannot directly shoot a holding through that box. Its spook the herd option supplies the holding-pressure route.

The holding offers two different kinds of progress: disable or remove a crew member now, or move Stampede toward a future holding hit. Neither option is especially cheap compared with specialized cards, but the flexibility can be useful in a teaching set or a mixed holding lineup.

Counterplay depends on the chosen route. Cover key crew from injury, while separately tracking the spook the herd queue. Do not let an erroneous card transcription turn the Totem into a two-whiskey general hit holding with an additional spook the herd option.

Current: starting cards 1; use 1. Patch up if the opponent has an exposed surviving holding. A destroyed holding cannot satisfy this condition, even with an empty column. The condition rewards maintaining pressure or an open enemy lane while repairing your side. It cannot patch up itself.

This creates an interesting opponent choice: place a defender to turn off your healing, or leave the holding exposed for other reasons. A newly placed enemy body can switch off the condition. Your Box Canyon can supply a turn of exposure, but you still need the healing target and holding readiness.

Starting cards 0; use 1. Deal normal hit if any Trouble resolved this turn. Either player's Trouble qualifies, including an opponent's Trouble you resolve through Telegraph Office. Stampede and zero-delay Trouble count. The condition is about resolution, not merely playing a Trouble into the queue or moving it into slot one.

Mountain Hideout rewards combining a Trouble's effect with an efficient shot. An immediate Poker Night or Ambush can switch it on during Actions; a queued Trouble resolving at the start can prepare it before you collect whiskey. Plan the extra shot while selecting targets for the Trouble.

Counterplay includes denying or delaying the Trouble resolution where possible, but do not assume a quiet visible queue makes the Mountain Hideout inactive: an immediate Trouble in hand can satisfy the condition. Its zero opening-card contribution means it benefits from partners that provide cards or reliable Trouble access.

Special reusable Trouble; normal launch delay 2. Stampede resolve into defender-chosen holding hit and return to their special area. They are launched or advanced by spook the herd effects, not by drawing them from the deck. Cover does not stop their holding hit. The queue and timing procedures appear in chapter 5.

Strategically, Stampede provide a dependable direction for cards that cannot otherwise hit holdings. The opponent can choose where early hit goes, so supplement the spook the herd plan with targeted attacks or enough repeated resolutions to remove that flexibility. Treat every visible spook the herd source as part of a possible same-turn countdown, including hand hock that has not yet been revealed.

Special reusable hand resource; take for 1, hock for 1 extra whiskey. It stores one future whiskey opportunity in card form. It is not a holding, crew member, ordinary Trouble, or eligible substitute for discard costs that explicitly exclude it.

Take it when one otherwise unusable whiskey remains and the following turn can use four. Do not buy it reflexively if spending that whiskey on a spook the herd or a crew member would matter more. It is especially useful before expensive deployments and two two-whiskey actions. The best time to save it is before the turn you need it; waiting until the critical turn merely trades one current whiskey for another.

Starting cards 1. Trait: your drifters gain a two-whiskey normal hit ability. Holding ability: pay 2 for a drifter. Gunsmith turns disposable cover into possible attackers and also supplies a replacement body. Its trait remains active while the holding is damaged; destroying the holding removes it.

Drifters still follow readiness rules. A drifter created this turn does not ordinarily attack immediately. A two-whiskey attack also leaves only one normal whiskey for everything else, so the holding does not automatically turn six drifters into six shots. Its value is flexible attack access from several positions, resilience through replacement, and a threat that does not depend on drawing Argo.

Counterplay can remove the holding, sweep drifters with injury, or force the owner to spend the two-whiskey budget on defense. Ordinary cover still limits the hit ability's targets.

Starting cards 1; use 2 to recruit a damaged enemy, or 2 to patch up. The recruited crew member changes sides and may be placed in a legal available position. It stays damaged and does not enter play again. The two abilities are alternatives under normal readiness, so recruitment followed by the holding's own restoration needs an explicit extra activation and enough whiskey.

Jailhouse converts an enemy's disabled engine into your future resource and removes one of their screens. Its threat changes injury strategy: an opponent may prefer to recover a valuable damaged crew member into hand rather than leave it exposed to recruitment.

Recruitment is not a way to retrigger Civil War Veteran / Buffalo Soldier Veteran, create Duelist / Wild Bill Hickok's drifter, or satisfy Bordello. Counterplay includes healing the crew member before the Jailhouse turn, removing Jailhouse, or making its owner unable to use the recruit profitably before the game ends.

Starting cards 1; trait. Your Stampede resolving generates an extra whiskey. The trigger rewards completed spooks the herd rather than merely launching or advancing the Trouble. Holding hit does not normally switch off the trait.

This makes the timing of a spook the herd economically important. A resolution during Actions can fund a follow-up play; a resolution during Trouble can add to the resources available for the coming action phase. Keep generated whiskey distinct from the ordinary supply and spent markers.

Robbers Roost fits a lineup with reliable spook the herd sources or repeated Stampede resolutions. Without a way to complete spooks the herd, it is a passive promise that may never pay. Counterplay against the spook the herd infrastructure can deny both holding hit and the bonus whiskey, while merely adding more holding screens does neither.

Starting cards 0; use 3. Destroy any enemy holding if you have at least six crew. The FAQ explicitly permits more than six through Boarding House. The crew are a condition, not a sacrifice payment.

The Ram turns a full board into a direct victory threat. Drifters count, as do damaged or newly entered crew. Three whiskey is the full ordinary turn budget, so generating the sixth crew member and activating the Ram in the same turn may require a cheap entry, a Trouble that already resolved, or extra whiskey.

Counterplay can be as small as removing one crew member before the critical turn, but the opponent may replace it cheaply. A full population plus an unspent Ram should be treated as a live holding-destruction threat regardless of how well your holdings are screened.

Starting cards 0; use 1. Use the hock effect of an eligible crew member that entered play this turn, without discarding that crew member. It turns entry into additional flexibility: a body can remain while its symbol also produces value. The holding cannot patch up itself from a patch up symbol.

The published preview describes the desire to use symbols without turning them into rigid factions. Strategically, consider both the crew member's battlefield effect and its hock before playing it. A cheap crew member with exactly the needed symbol can become more useful than a prestigious expensive card.

Counterplay can pressure the holding's zero-card opening or disrupt repeated entries. Jailhouse recruitment does not supply a fresh entry. A returned and replayed crew member does, but its play cost and the Market's own activation must both be paid.

The printed target is “a crew member,” without an explicit controller restriction. Whether an unusual opposing entry during your turn qualifies remains a separate interpretation question; the card scan does not establish a designer ruling on that corner case.

Starting cards 1; use 3. Destroy the enemies in one column, hit its holding, then destroy Rockslide Ridge. The crew removal ignores their cover through the all-enemies scope. If the holding hit destroys the opponent's final holding, victory occurs before Rockslide Ridge destroys itself.

Rockslide Ridge is a powerful one-shot opening or finisher, not a repeatable hit engine. Its cost includes losing one of your own holdings, so a spectacular visual wipe can still leave you behind. The best target often combines valuable crew with a damaged holding.

Counterplay includes avoiding a crowded decisive lane, keeping the key holding undamaged, or forcing Rockslide Ridge to be used defensively. If your last holding is damaged, a surviving Rockslide Ridge can threaten it through all ordinary screens.

Starting cards 1; use 2. Hit any enemy holding if the opponent has no drifters, then offer them a drifter through the effect. The new body can shut off another use of the same attack condition. If their board is full, the FAQ permits replacement to make room; gaining the drifter remains optional under the normal rule.

This creates a repeated tactical bargain. The opponent may accept a protective body to stop the next Bounty Office shot, while you may then remove that drifter to reopen the condition. A healthy drifter is only one injury away from destruction, but removing it still takes an effect.

With Vera, do not assume two immediate holding hits: recheck whether the first resolution left the opponent with a drifter. The condition is based on their population, not yours.

Starting cards 1; use 1. Hit one of your own undamaged cards, then patch up another legal damaged card. It transfers health between useful assets at a whiskey cost. The self-harm is expressly authorized; an ordinary hit hock would not be.

The undamaged requirement prevents feeding an already damaged crew member to obtain the patch up through this exact effect. A healthy expendable crew member can be wounded to repair a crucial holding or patch up a trait. The Totem cannot use the resulting patch up on itself under the general self-restoration rule.

Consider the full change in threat. Injuring your own only attacker to repair a minor holding may cost more than it saves. Counterplay can exploit the supply of healthy payment cards or force hit onto several important assets faster than one activation can repair them.

Starting cards 1; use 1. Sacrifice one of your crew, then deal normal hit. It is a holding-based conversion from bodies to attacks, resembling Hellfire Preacher / Revival Sister's role but with a whiskey cost and the durability/readiness behavior of a holding.

Drifters and spent entry-effect crew are useful fuel. A damaged holding can still activate, so merely injuring Revival Tent does not deny the next sacrifice shot. Its attack follows ordinary cover; it is not Dynamite Shack's any-card access.

Counterplay can reduce available fodder, keep cheap screens in front of valuable targets, or destroy the holding when it is already damaged. When drafting, pair it with a realistic body supply rather than treating every future hand as an endless source of free sacrifices.

Starting cards 1; use 2 plus discard 5 non-Flask cards. Destroy any enemy battlefield card of the allowed type, including a covered holding. This exchanges a large hand resource for precise, decisive removal.

The five-card payment is enormous if it does not end the game or prevent immediate defeat. Saving five cards while falling behind on the board can be a trap. Conversely, a hand that seems passive may conceal an unavoidable final-holding destruction once the Ray is ready and funded.

Counterplay should respect the hand threshold. Pressure that forces discards or hock use can move the opponent below the required five cards. More crew in front of your holding do not solve an any-card attack. The Hip Flask cannot serve as one of the five renewable payments.

Starting cards 1; use 2 to spook the herd; trait on your Stampede resolving. The trait pushes opposing Trouble backward where they can legally move. This couples holding pressure with Trouble disruption. A blocked Trouble remains in its position rather than disappearing.

The ideal turn completes a spook the herd while delaying a Trouble that would otherwise spoil your next attack. Do not activate the spook the herd mode without checking the queue: a blocked Stampede advance may fail to reach the resolution that triggers the disruption.

The trait survives hit to the holding. Counterplay can attack the spook the herd sources, use immediate Trouble, or exploit a Trouble already at the back of a blocked queue. The Derby does not cancel a Trouble permanently; it buys time when movement is possible.

Starting cards 1; use 3. Draw two cards. Unlike General Store, this is net hand growth rather than drawing two and returning one to discard. The price is your full ordinary whiskey budget.

This is strongest in a quiet position where you can afford to invest in future options, or where extra whiskey lets you draw and still answer a threat. It can feed discard-hungry holdings or a Land Office plan. It is weak when spending the whole turn on cards leaves a holding to die.

Counterplay is direct pressure. Make the owner choose between drawing two and surviving. Do not claim the Office is always superior to ordinary draw: the one remaining whiskey after a normal two-whiskey draw can be the most important action of the turn.

Starting cards 1; use 1 for the movement-and-patch up effect, or 2 to spook the herd. Move your damaged crew member from another column into this holding's column and patch up it. The published rulings explicitly rules out healing someone already in the Hospital column by claiming a zero-distance move. The FAQ also requires room in the destination, with normal insertion around an existing crew member.

The column requirement is a deliberate limitation on convenient repeated healing. A hospital lane crowded with two crew cannot simply accept a third under normal capacity. Restoring the crew member does not ordinarily make it ready.

Its spook the herd alternative is useful when no legal repair exists. Counterplay may involve filling the hospital's tactical obligations, threatening crew in ways movement cannot solve, or attacking holdings directly. Do not treat it as an unrestricted one-whiskey patch up icon for any card.

Starting cards 0; starts one space forward; use 3 for three drifters. A crew member can occupy the covered position behind it. The drifter ability supplies several bodies, subject to capacity and optional gain rules. When Wagon Fort is destroyed, return the burned-out holding to the back and place the crew in front.

Wagon Fort combines unusual geometry with a population engine. It can shelter a useful crew member while itself taking ordinary hit, and its large drifter burst can support Bunkhouse or Timber Ram. Three whiskey for population is a major commitment; an imminent Cholera can erase the new bodies.

Counterplay includes any-target removal against the covered engine or concentrated holding hit against Wagon Fort. Its forward position is not extra holding health, and a destroyed Wagon Fort does not remain in the middle as an indestructible screen.

Starting cards 1; use 1. Hire a drifter if the opponent has an exposed surviving holding. It rewards maintaining access to the enemy holding row and converts that pressure into your own cover or population. A damaged enemy holding behind a crew member is still covered and does not satisfy the condition. A destroyed holding also fails the condition, even when its column is empty.

Free Homestead can support a broad board while your attacks keep one enemy lane open. With a sacrifice engine, a newly generated drifter can become another resource. With Timber Ram, a single extra body may cross the decisive threshold.

Counterplay creates a tradeoff: putting a body in front of the open holding can stop the drifter production, but costs a card or effect. Box Canyon temporarily changes the condition, so the owner can sometimes manufacture the necessary exposure for one turn.

Starting cards 2; use 1 to spook the herd, launching Stampede at slot 3 when it places them. If Stampede are already in the queue, the spook the herd performs its ordinary advance rather than restarting them. The slower launch balances a holding that contributes more opening cards than Cattle Ranch.

Its value depends on whether another source can launch Stampede at the normal position first. Coal Yard can then serve as an advance source without imposing a new slot-3 launch. Queue congestion remains important.

Zeto overrides the launch delay when this is the first Trouble played that turn: Stampede resolves immediately. This is explicitly confirmed by the published rulings; see case B. Later launches, or launches without Zeto's active trait, use position three. Counterplay can disable Zeto before the turn or exploit that slower ordinary launch.

Starting cards 0; use 2. Destroy an exposed enemy crew member, then the opponent may use its ability without the normal whiskey payment. Destruction occurs first. The FAQ details Hellfire Preacher / Revival Sister, Sarah Winnemucca / Getaway Rider, Bartender / Piano Player, and Con Man / Bass Reeves because those outcomes are unintuitive.

Evaluate both halves before choosing the victim. Removing a dangerous permanent engine may still be worth allowing one final effect. Giving an opponent a free Molgur-like ability can be catastrophic if it destroys your last holding; choosing a crew member with an irrelevant ability may be nearly free removal.

Counterplay can arrange your exposed crew so every attractive Gallows victim has a painful final ability. Do not assume readiness blocks the special permission, and do not attempt to self-rescue a Team that has already been destroyed.

Starting cards 1; use 1 plus discard two non-Flask hand cards. Discard both cards before optionally using either or both hock effects in either order, then deal normal hit. Both discard payments are required even when you want only one hock symbol; a card drawn by the first hock effect cannot replace either payment.

Its strength is compression. A hock injury can clear a screen before the final hit; a patch up can save a holding; a spook the herd can resolve Stampede and activate another condition. Plan the order of the two hock effects rather than resolving them arbitrarily.

Counterplay can pressure the owner's hand or alter cover so the final hit has less value. Treat the two discarded cards as a real expenditure. The holding does not create their normal played abilities, and using both hock effects does not mean playing two Trouble.

Starting cards 2; use 2. Destroy all of your crew in this column, then deal normal hit. You can fire with no crew in the column: the published preview explains the intended four-crew member board and the earlier version that prohibited deploying crew in this lane. This supplies direct design support for the empty-column use previously retained as case D.

This encourages an exposed holding or a column containing expendable crew. It also offers a way to clear your own damaged bodies while attacking, but sacrifices every crew member in that lane rather than choosing just one. Do not place your most valuable covered engine there and forget the future cost.

Counterplay can take advantage of the holding's exposure. A two-card opening contribution can make it useful even if the attack is not used every turn. Its destruction of your crew is a printed exception to the normal no-friendly-fire rule.

Starting cards 1; use 1. Patch up a damaged friendly crew member, then discard the top three deck cards. If any has wound hock, replace that crew member with a drifter and gain one extra whiskey. The published rulings preview describes the one-whiskey activation and refund risk. The replacement destroys the crew member and creates a new drifter in exactly the same position.

This is risky recovery. The result can preserve a body while losing the valuable identity you hoped to patch up. It is more attractive when the crew member is expendable or when the refund and new entry help another plan. The trigger checks wound hock, not drifter hock; that distinction was wrong in one secondary explanation reviewed for this book.

Counterplay should not assume the target always survives as its original crew member. The holding's randomness may help or hurt its owner. Avoid describing its best outcome as a guaranteed cheap healing engine.

Starting cards 0; use 2 to hire a drifter. Trait: inspect your own drifters and pay a revealed crew member's cost to flip it into play ready; the card remains in place. Only a crew member can be developed this way; a Trouble remains a drifter until another effect changes its status. The entry counts for relevant traits and holding conditions. The two-whiskey drifter activation and the revealed crew member's play cost are separate payments; paying for a drifter does not also pay to develop it.

Wanted Poster Board converts hidden bodies into a reserve of known possible attackers. Unlike original Breaking Pen, it lets you decide whether the revealed crew member is worth paying for before developing it. The position is fixed, so a valuable engine may emerge in an exposed slot.

Counterplay includes removing drifters before they are developed, attacking Wanted Poster Board, or forcing the owner to use whiskey defensively. Inspection is private. With Wagon Fort or Gold Rush, place all incoming drifters before inspecting their faces. You cannot use an early peek to decide where the next drifter goes or which newly placed drifter to replace.

Starting cards 1; use 1 to patch up after one of your cards was damaged or destroyed during your own turn. The current FAQ includes full-board replacement destruction. Hit from the opponent's preceding turn does not qualify. The holding cannot patch up itself.

It works with sacrifice holdings, Doc Holliday / Laudanum Doctor's self-hit, Packer's Cabin, and other deliberate costs that your plan already wants to pay. The best use recovers an important holding or trait after extracting value from a less important asset.

Do not create a harmful trigger merely to use an available ability. Damaging a healthy engine so you can repair an irrelevant crew member is not progress. Counterplay can focus on the Boot Hill itself or make the owner choose among several urgent restoration targets after only one triggering sequence.

Starting cards 1; use 1 to remove a burned-out holding and deal normal hit, or 2 to spook the herd. The removed holding may belong to either player. Its former slot can then hold a crew member, producing a three-crew member column. The one-whiskey hit requires the burned out-removal step; it is not an unconditional one-whiskey gun from turn one.

The published rulings explains that the burned out prerequisite prevents certain excessively fast openings. Strategically, removing your own burned out can increase your cover or population ceiling, while removing an enemy burned out gives them more space and changes which burned-out holdings physically remain. Whether a removed holding still counts for a particular burned out-dependent benefit is a separate rules question, not settled merely by reading the removal ability.

Track removed holdings separately from face-down burned-out holdings still on the board. Population thresholds, Widow with a Shotgun / Homestead Defender placement, Homestead Cabin discounts, and Cannonade counts should not be handled with a vague memory that “a holding died somewhere.” The spook the herd option remains useful when no removable burned out exists.

Starting cards 1; use 1. If you have a drifter, gain another drifter or produce a spook the herd. The existing drifter is a condition, not automatically a sacrifice. This is one printed ability with a choice of result, not two separate ability boxes; ordinary readiness means you choose one result per activation.

The Club grows a board while a drifter survives and can switch from growth to holding pressure without changing the card. It fits Bunkhouse, Gunsmith, and Timber Ram plans. A single starting drifter can therefore become the seed of a much larger resource system.

Counterplay often begins by removing the final drifter before the owner's turn. But a drifter hock or another holding may restart the engine, so count their alternative sources. Do not overcommit to removing all faceup crew while leaving the cheap drifter that keeps the Club operating.

Starting cards 1; use 2 to patch up while undamaged, or 2 to deal normal hit while damaged. Unlike a crew member, the damaged holding still has an available role, and the hit state changes which ability condition is satisfied. Both modes cost the same two whiskey.

The Village complicates target selection for the opponent. A first hit can switch it from support to offense; a second destroys it. As its owner, do not automatically patch up it simply because it is sideways. You may prefer the attacking mode for the current race.

Its own patch up cannot heal the Village, and its undamaged condition must be satisfied before choosing that mode. Counterplay may call for two hit effects in one turn so the opponent never enjoys the damaged attack mode, or for leaving it healthy when its healing is less threatening.

Starting cards 1; use 1. Ready your other holdings and your undamaged crew. Damaged faceup holdings are included; damaged crew are not. The scope is easy to misread in a flattened transcription. The FAQ confirms that newly entered, patched up, and previously used eligible cards can be readied. Spent whiskey is not refunded.

Chuckwagon converts whiskey into additional activation opportunities. A ready Molgur can destroy a holding for one, the Plant can ready it for one, and Molgur can destroy another for one: three whiskey with both cards already established. The Plant does not ready itself.

Counterplay targets the valuable beneficiary or the Plant, or constrains the owner's whiskey. Repeated readiness has little value when the available abilities are too expensive to pay again. Cheap and zero-cost abilities make this holding much more dangerous.

Starting cards 2; use 0 plus discard three non-Flask hand cards, then draw two cards. The zero-whiskey cost is verified against the printed card. It still uses the holding's activation and requires all three hand cards; zero whiskey does not mean an unlimited exchange.

The strategic purpose is hand conversion rather than raw card advantage. You give up more cards than you retain but may turn unusable options into the specific hock or play needed now. Because the activation costs no whiskey, you can still spend the normal three-whiskey budget after the exchange. That exchange is sensible only when quality matters more than quantity, or when the deck-drawing objective makes the draws especially valuable.

Counterplay can exploit the reduced hand afterward. Do not use the discarded cards' hock effects unless an effect explicitly authorizes them; this is not Pawn Shop. Do not feed the Depot a Hip Flask when the printed exclusion forbids it.

Starting cards 1; use 1. Return one of your crew that did not enter this turn to hand. For a faceup crew member, neither that card nor another copy may be put into play that turn. A returned drifter has the confirmed exception below. The restriction covers entry through other effects, not just the normal Play Card action.

This is recovery for future turns, not Sarah Winnemucca / Getaway Rider's unrestricted same-turn entry loop. It can save a damaged expensive crew member, uncover a drifter's real card, or remove a body from a strategically awkward slot. The immediate cost may be exposing a holding and forgoing the recovered crew member's current activation.

Counterplay pressures the time gap before replay. If the opponent spends whiskey to recover their only screen, a direct attack route may become available. Remember the restriction on another copy; keeping a second identical crew member in hand does not automatically bypass the Post's limit.

The published rulings explicitly exempts a returned drifter: its underlying card may be played faceup that turn, and returning it does not forbid other drifters. Apply the copy restriction when the returned object was a faceup crew member; do not secretly attach it to a drifter's hidden card identity.

Starting cards 1; use 2. All battlefield cards on both sides are exposed for the rest of the turn. Unlike Box Canyon's opponent-only exposure, the broad wording also opens your own side. The effect changes legal targets; it does not hit anything by itself.

Lookout Ridge can turn ordinary hit, wound, and destroy abilities into precise attacks on sheltered targets. Its two-whiskey activation leaves one normal whiskey, so plan a cheap follow-up or an extra-whiskey source before exposing everything. Its downside matters with Duelist / Wild Bill Hickok, Dance Hall, Gallows, or another effect that gives the opponent an action during your turn: your formerly covered cards may now be valid targets too.

Counterplay usually happens before the exposure turn by disabling attackers or winning the race. Simply stacking more screens does not prevent the effect. When the turn ends, the temporary exposure ends and normal geometry matters again.

Starting cards 1; use 1. Deal normal hit if both players have a crew member, then the opponent wounds one of your exposed crew. The retaliation is injury, so it affects crew rather than holdings. The condition is about both players having a crew member; drifters count.

This creates an asymmetric exchange: your hit may hit a holding, while the return effect cannot. It can therefore be attractive when the opponent's wound has only a disposable screen to hit. It is less attractive when your exposed key trait crew member would be disabled.

As with Duelist / Wild Bill Hickok, analyze the returned effect under the actual targeting conditions, especially during Lookout Ridge exposure. Do not change the opponent's injury into a free holding hit or assume they must wound the crew member you would prefer. Lookout Ridge's two-whiskey activation plus Dance Hall's one-whiskey attack uses the ordinary three-whiskey budget, but also exposes your own crew to the retaliation.

Its flexibility is strongest when several symbols would be useful. A random reveal is a poor foundation for a line that must hit one exact result unless you know the top card legally. Drifter destruction can change what is on top, but a hidden drifter's face is still unknown unless another effect revealed it.

Counterplay should weigh the actual distribution of useful outcomes rather than treating the Lab as guaranteed hit or healing. Its zero opening-card contribution is another reason to select partners with enough initial hand resources.

It does not reduce the activation costs of Cattle Ranch, Rustler / Drover, other spook the herd-producing abilities, or Cattlemen's Club's own two-whiskey spook the herd. The spook the herd ability was absent from the earlier extracted-text summary but is clear on the physical card.

Cattlemen's Club can turn cheap Trouble into efficient setup actions and reduce the extra-whiskey burden of Cannonade. A zero-cost Trouble remains subject to its queue placement unless it has delay 0 or another effect changes that delay. Discounting a card is not the same as making it immediate.

Its spook the herd gives it an active pressure role even when the hand contains no worthwhile Trouble. With three normal whiskey, you can play a printed two-whiskey Trouble for one and then pay two to spook the herd, provided the Trouble and Stampede each have a legal queue placement or advance. Conversely, spending all three whiskey on a discounted Cannonade leaves no normal whiskey for the spook the herd. Plan the queue as well as the discount.

Counterplay can attack the holding or disrupt the Trouble themselves. A crew member-heavy hand may not exploit the trait immediately, but does not remove the spook the herd option. Its zero starting-card contribution makes opening-hand support from the other two holdings valuable; draft it for a plausible Trouble-and-spook the herd plan rather than valuing the discount in isolation.
